requiredPages.title: Project Profile
requiredPages.purpose: Identify the asset, developer or promoter, address, district, city, project ID, asset type, scale, height or floors, completion status, evidence date, image and source.

requiredPages.title: Project Scope & Products
requiredPages.purpose: Residential: unit mix, bedrooms, floor areas, prices and payment terms. Commercial: office/retail/industrial space types, floor areas, use by level, unit count, lease/sale availability and booking terms.

requiredPages.title: Development & Delivery
requiredPages.purpose: Show developer, construction timeline, completion evidence, delivery status, whole-project scope, facilities, infrastructure and six nearby City Jewels or comparable assets.

requiredPages.title: Price & Market Intelligence
requiredPages.purpose: Show starting price or rent, lowest published price per m², price by product/space type, three best comparables, calculation basis, value advantage or premium, and disclosed project value.

requiredPages.title: Location & Verification
requiredPages.purpose: Include a project pin map and a local-area map, district/sector/cell/address, nearby schools/universities, transport stops, landmarks, source register and verification checklist.

evidenceRules: Do not fabricate a project ID. Use an existing register identifier or label the identifier as a Taiseel internal ID.
A developer-announced count such as 40+ must remain 40+; do not silently convert it to 40.
Do not label commercial office areas as bedrooms or residential units.
Do not report a building height in metres unless an authoritative source publishes it; floor count is not a height measurement.
Keep developer marketing claims separate from independently verified facts.
Distinguish current asking rent, sale asking price, launch price, transaction price, estimate and historical plan.
Always show the currency, area basis, and whether a rent is per month or per year.
Never infer project value from gross floor area and asking rent without explicit valuation assumptions; state not disclosed when no defensible valuation is available.
Mark unit availability, booking fees, deposits and payment terms as unverified or not published when sources do not establish them.
Distances must identify the source and method. Distinguish developer-published distances, straight-line estimates and routed travel distances.
Every important claim needs a project-specific source and, where relevant, an as-of date.
City Jewels must be real named buildings, developments or civic/business anchors relevant to the project location; distinguish them from direct price comparables.
Keep the five page slots and order identical across all reports.
Project facts and sources remain separate; never copy one project's facts into another.
Describe neighbourhoods through verifiable physical facts such as access, services, transport, planning and amenities; do not infer who belongs in an area.
Treat subjective phrases such as safe, family-friendly, exclusive or best neighbourhood as attributed opinion unless supported by a relevant, clearly described dataset.
visualRules: Every project study uses five pages in the same order: Project Profile; Project Scope & Products; Development & Delivery; Price & Market Intelligence; Location & Verification.
Use the same 1280 by 720 page frame, typography scale, navy/gold palette, table treatment, evidence labels and footer system.
Use one project-specific image on the cover only when its URL and source are recorded; otherwise show an explicit image-not-yet-attached state.
Use the same two-map pattern on the location page: a project map and a surrounding-area context map.
Keep City Jewels separate from direct price comparables; label wider-district and city-wide references as such.
genericFallbackRules: Show the Taiseel internal project ID; do not present it as a public developer ID.
Pass and display all available register facts: developer, owner, location hierarchy, project scale labels, land area, project start, completion, project route, UPI, image and source links.
Display a stored image only when the image URL is valid HTTP(S); otherwise show an explicit placeholder.
Show an exact project pin only when numeric latitude and longitude exist and location precision is address-coordinate or parcel-upi.
For district or sector precision, display an administrative-area search map labelled area context only; never style it as an exact parcel or entrance pin.
Show missing unit/space mix, prices, payment terms, booking, height, occupancy and current availability as not published, not verified or not established.
Never add nearby facilities or comparables to the fallback unless those names and evidence are attached to that project record.

pageRules: Every dedicated report has exactly five pages, in pageSequence order.
Every page declares one of the four assetTypes in data-report-type.
All reports load report-system.css; project files supply facts, evidence and imagery only.
Page-specific headlines may be descriptive, but the section label and page number stay canonical.
The generic fallback derives asset type from the project category and labels mixed-use projects as both residential and commercial.

rules: Use 'space' or the named commercial use for offices, shops, retail, dining and other commercial areas; do not describe them as bedrooms.
Use 'bedrooms' only for residential product schedules.
Use 'room count' for hotels and serviced accommodation where the source reports rooms.
Keep marketing statements, government records, independent verification and Taiseel calculations visibly distinct.
Use 'not published' when no source publishes a fact; use 'not established' when available sources do not resolve it.
Use 'availability unverified' unless current inventory is confirmed by a responsible seller or operator.
For rent, show currency, per-square-metre basis and billing period; never compare rent with sale price as if they were the same measure.
For calculated values, show the source inputs, formula and date; do not present an estimate as a transaction or formal valuation.
Describe neighbourhoods through verifiable physical facts such as access, services, transport, planning and amenities; do not infer who belongs in an area.
Treat subjective phrases such as safe, family-friendly, exclusive or best neighbourhood as attributed opinion unless supported by a relevant, clearly described dataset.
